hooks.text: One tiny moon looks like a jigsaw puzzle glued back together.
This moon of Uranus has a cliff twelve miles deep.
This moon is smaller than Texas but has solar system's deepest canyons.

title: The Moon That Was Smashed to Pieces
description: Explore the mystery of Miranda, a moon of Uranus with the solar system's deepest canyons and a surface that defies logic.

beats.text: One tiny moon looks like a jigsaw puzzle glued back together.
beats.visual: Voyager 2 image of the Uranian moon Miranda, 1986

beats.text: When Voyager 2 reached Uranus in 1986, scientists expected its moon Miranda to be a boring ice-ball.
beats.visual: artist's concept of Voyager 2 at the planet Uranus, 1986

beats.text: Instead, they found a 'Frankenstein' world of mismatched geological blocks and a massive V-shaped scar.
beats.visual: mosaic of Miranda showing mismatched terrain types, Voyager 2

beats.text: Miranda’s surface features Verona Rupes, a staggering cliff reaching up to twelve miles deep.
beats.visual: high-resolution view of the Verona Rupes cliff on Miranda, 1986

beats.text: That is twelve times deeper than the Grand Canyon, on a world barely the size of Texas.
beats.visual: aerial photograph of the Grand Canyon, Arizona

beats.text: One leading theory suggests this chaotic moon was shattered by impacts multiple times before reassembling.
beats.visual: artist's concept of a moon being shattered by a giant impact

beats.text: Alternatively, extreme tidal heating from Uranus might have churned the moon's icy interior into these bizarre shapes.
beats.visual: diagram showing tidal heating in a moon's interior

beats.text: Since we have only photographed its southern half, the rest of the jigsaw puzzle remains a mystery.
beats.visual: Voyager 2 photograph of Miranda's southern hemisphere

better_than_last: Implemented a mystery structure that reveals the 'shattered and reassembled' theory as the solution to the visual puzzle presented in the hook.
